parole.testo: From Middle High German kōsen, from Old High German kōson, ultimately borrowed from Latin causa.
18th century, from Latin crassus. See English crass for more.

parole.significato: creation (all that exists, as being created by God)
parole.testo: In part directly from Latin creātiō, in part through French création.
Borrowed from Latin creātor. Doublet of Kreateur.

parole.significato: to design; to shape; to create (a composition, a fashion line, etc.)
parole.testo: From French créer (from Latin creō) + -ieren. Compare Hunsrik krieere.
From Middle High German kriuze, from Old High German kruzi, from Latin crux (gen. crucis).
Kreuz (“cross”) + Zeichen (“sign”). Calque of Latin signum crucis.

parole.significato: crystal in the sense of mineral and its molecular structure ("array of atoms"), not in the sense of glass / glassware (…
parole.testo: From Middle High German kristal, kristalle, from Old High German cristalla, from Latin crystallum, from Ancient Greek κρύσταλλος (krústallos, “ice”). Cognate with Vilamovian kryśtaoł.
Borrowed from Latin critērium, critērion, from Ancient Greek κριτήριον (kritḗrion).
Learned borrowing from Latin crocus, from Ancient Greek κρόκος (krókos).
From Old High German krusta, borrowed from Latin crusta.
Borrowed from Latin crypta, from Ancient Greek κρυπτή (kruptḗ), female form of the adjective κρυπτός (kruptós).
Borrowed from Latin Croesus, from Ancient Greek Κροῖσος (Kroîsos).

parole.significato: curiosity (unique or extraordinary object which arouses interest)
parole.testo: From Latin cūriōsum, neuter singular of cūriōsus.
Derived from Latin cursus. Cognate with Russian курс (kurs), French cours, French course, English course etc. Doublet of Korso.

17th century, backformation from Kursive, from Latin (scriptura) cursiva. The adjective is mainly a term of printing in German, but the noun Kursive is also common for (styles of) cursive handwriting.

parole.significato: spontaneously, suddenly, on the spot (without much prior deliberation or preparation)
parole.testo: Univerbation of kurzer + Hand, calque of Latin brevī manū.
Borrowed from Latin custōs. Compare (obsolete) English custos (literally “warden”).
From Middle High German kevje, from Old High German chevia, from Latin cavea (“cage”).

From Middle High German korper, körper, körpel, from Latin corpor-, inflected stem of corpus. The word displaced first the predecessor of German Leiche, Leichnam (now “corpse”) and later on Leib (now dated, literary, religious). Doublet of Korpus, Korps. parole.significato: a fairly tall tub or bucket, especially one with two handles on the sides (rather than a pail)
parole.testo: From Middle High German kübel, from Old High German kubilo, a vinicultural loan from Latin cūpula. Doublet of Kuppel.

parole.significato: lip balm; chapstick (a plastic stick including a substance that is applied to the lips to relieve dry lips)
parole.testo: From the brand name Labello, apparently a portmanteau word of Latin labium (“lip”) + bellus (“beautiful”), or similar forms in Romance languages such as Italian labbro + bello.
Clipping of Laboratorium, from Latin labōrātōrium.

parole.significato: to work in a laboratory, to apply chemistry on a specific thing

parole.testo: From Middle High German leie, leige, from Old High German leigo, a borrowing of Latin lāicus.
18th century, from Latin lapidarius, after French lapidaire.
From Latin lapis lazuli, which see.

Pseudo-Latinism, derived from Lappen (“cloth, rag”) + Latin -ālia (neuter plural of relational adjective suffix), 17th c.. Initially as the plural Lappalia, then showing the Germanized plural Lappalien, then back-forming a feminine singular.

parole.significato: larva (early stage of growth for some insects and amphibians)
parole.testo: From Middle High German larve, from Latin lārva (“ghost; mask”).
In the 20th century, from Latin laterālis.

parole.significato: lantern (casing for a light source, fashioned from transparent material)
parole.testo: From Middle High German laterne, lanterne, from Latin lanterna with possible influence from French lanterne, from Ancient Greek λαμπτήρ (lamptḗr).

From Middle High German latech, leteche, from Old High German latihha, lattuhha, from Latin lactuca (“lettuce”). Possibly through a Proto-West Germanic *ladukā ~ *lahtukā, though the wide variety of West Germanic forms makes such a reconstruction difficult.
Ultimately from Latin laqueus. Doublet of Lasso.

Via Middle High German lūne (“moon, changing mood, disposition”), borrowed from Latin lūna (“moon”). The semantic association of "moon" to "mood" is based on the similarity of the changing phases of the moon to the changing moods of a person (DWDS).
Learned borrowing from Latin lavābō (“I will wash”), lavāre, the first word of psalm 26,6.
From Leben + -s- + Lauf, a calque of Latin curriculum vītae. Similar to Dutch levensloop.
Learned borrowing from Latin lēgālis (“legal”), from lēx (“law”).

parole.significato: legacy, a detachment of certain items of the heritage
legitimate, justified by law, morals or custom
parole.testo: 18th century, from Latin lēgitimus in legal parlance. The form (especially the final stress) is probably influenced by French légitime.
From Latin legitimare, ultimately from lēgitimus (“lawful, legal, legitimate”); equivalent to legitim + -ieren (“-ize, -ify”).
17th century, from Leiden (“suffering”) + -schaft, a calque of Latin passio. Compare Dutch lijdenschap.
From Middle High German līre, from Old High German līra, from Latin lyra, from Ancient Greek λύρα (lúra).

parole.significato: lesson (chapter of a textbook, section of a course)
parole.testo: From Middle High German lectiōn (13th c.), relatinized form of older lecze, letze, from Old High German lekza (9th c.), a borrowing from Latin lēctiō. Compare Dutch les, Swedish läxa.

parole.significato: reviser, proofreader (a person who proofreads or corrects written material)

parole.testo: From the Latin lemma, from the Ancient Greek λῆμμᾰ (lêmmă).
Borrowed from Latin lepra or Koine Greek λέπρα (lépra).
From Middle High German lettener, lecter, from Latin lectorium.

parole.significato: league (historic unit of measurement, especially the Roman league)

parole.testo: From Latin līberālis (“befitting a freeman”), from līber (“free”).

Borrowed from Latin libīdō. The usual stress on the first syllable probably from a generalisation of the tendency that penultimate Latin -i- is short; perhaps also reinforced by association with Liebe (“love”), though this is speculative.
From Middle High German lilje, from Old High German lilia, from Latin lilia.
From Latin limitare or else French limiter.
15th century, learned borrowing from Latin līneāle.

parole.significato: linear (long and narrow, with nearly parallel sides)

parole.significato: linear (long and narrow, with nearly parallel sides)
parole.testo: From Latin līneālis; by surface analysis, lineal + -isch. Doublet of linearisch.

parole.significato: linear (having the form of a line; straight or roughly straight; following a direct course)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin līneāris. Doublet of lineal.

parole.significato: linear (pertaining to polynomials of degree one)
parole.testo: From Latin līneāris; by surface analysis, linear + -isch. Doublet of linealisch.
Derived from Latin lingua (“language”) + -ist. Popularised in the 20th century under influence of English linguist, whence it may also have been borrowed in the 16th century.

From Middle High German linse, from Old High German linsa, likely a borrowing from an unidentified source. Compare Latin lēns, Lithuanian lęšis, and Old Church Slavonic лѧща (lęšta) sounding too similar for a coincidence, however different enough to prohibit reconstruction of a common PIE protoform.

parole.significato: man of letters, author (male or of unspecified gender)
literature (written works collectively, often about a certain topic, in a certain language etc.)
ornamental cord or fabric (braided or twisted); gimp; braid; trim
parole.testo: From Middle High German litze, possibly through a Romance form eventually from Latin līcia, plural of līcium. Compare French lisse, Italian liccio.
Borrowed from Latin logica, from Ancient Greek λογική (logikḗ, “logic”).
From Latin logicus, with assimilation to native suffix -isch.
From Latin locālis (“local”), from locus (“place, spot, location”).

From Middle High German lōrber, from Old High German lōrberi, from lōr (“laurel”) + beri (“berry”), the former from Latin laurus. The compound originally referred to the laurel's fruit or berry, which is now distinguished as Lorbeere (but fairly rare).
Borrowed from Latin lotos, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós).

parole.significato: to locate, to posit the place of

parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism from luftig + Latin -icus, -us, originally student slang.

parole.significato: to win, to profit by means of
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lucrō, from lucrum (“profit”), + -ieren.

parole.significato: meat from the loin of an animal (particularly, beef or pork)
parole.testo: From Middle High German lumbel, from Old High German lumbal (8th c.), borrowed from Latin lumbulus, diminutive of lumbus (“loin”).

parole.significato: lymph (the fluid carried by the lymphatic system)

In the literal sense inherited from Middle High German lewenzan, equivalent to Löwe (“lion”) + -n- + Zahn (“tooth”). The botanic sense is a 16th-century calque of Latin dēns leōnis, whence also English dandelion.

parole.significato: magister; an academic degree usually comparable to an M.A. or M.Sc.
parole.testo: From Middle High German magister, from Old High German magister, a learned borrowing from Latin magister. Doublet of Maestro, Master, and Meister.

parole.significato: May (the fifth month of the Gregorian calendar, following April and preceding June)
parole.testo: From Middle High German meie, from Old High German meio, from Latin (mensis) Maius, the Italic goddess of growth.
From Middle High German makel, borrowed from Latin macula. Related to Makulatur.

Borrowed from Latin mandātum, from mandō (“to command”).
From Middle High German mange, mangel, from Latin manganum, from Ancient Greek μάγγᾰνον (mángănon).

parole.significato: for there to be a lack [with dative ‘to someone/something’ and an (+ dative) ‘of something’] (idiomatically translated…
parole.testo: From Old High German mangolōn, from Latin mancō.
16th century, from Latin mania, from Ancient Greek μανία (manía).

parole.significato: mare (such as the large black plains on the Moon)

Borrowed from Latin marīnus; cf. French marin.
Borrowed from Latin marmor, from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros, “marble, crystalline rock”). Doublet of Murmel.
Middle High German marter, from Old High German martira, from ecclesiastical Latin martyrium.

parole.significato: Martinmas (feast day of St Martin of Tours)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Martini, genitive of Latin Martinus (“Martin”).
In the grammatical sense (since 15th c.) from Latin masculīnus. Broader use (chiefly since 19th c.) after French masculin.
From Middle High German masse, from Late Old High German massa, from Latin massa.
From Latin māteriālis. Doublet of materiell.
Borrowed from Latin mātrīx. Doublet of Matrize.

From Latin melancholicus, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολικός (melankholikós, “atrabilious, impulsive, of atrabilious or melancholic temperament”), from μελαγχολία (melankholía, “melancholy”). By surface analysis, Melancholie + -isch.

parole.significato: melody, tune (sequence of notes that makes up a musical phrase)
parole.testo: From Middle High German melodīe, from Latin melodia, from Ancient Greek μελῳδίᾱ (melōidíā). Since the 16th century, the inherited form Melodei was increasingly readapted to the Latin and to French mélodie.

parole.significato: academic fencing (fencing practiced by some student corporations)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mēnsūra (“measure”). In the context of fencing, the term originally denoted the distance that two fencers had to stand from one another.
Inherited from Middle High German messe, from Old High German missa, itself from Latin missa.

parole.significato: The Messiah / messiah (Jesus Christ, Jesus the Messiah, Jesus the Christ).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Messīās, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek Μεσσίας (Messías), from Aramaic משיחא (məšīḥā), from Biblical Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (māšîaḥ, “anointed”).
From Middle High German metalle, from Latin metallum (14th century).
From Latin metaphysica, from Byzantine Greek μεταφυσική (metaphusikḗ). By surface analysis, meta- + Physik.

parole.significato: meteor (streak of light caused by extraterrestrial matter entering the atmosphere)

From Latin methodicus, from Ancient Greek μεθοδικός (methodikós). Morphologically analyzable as Methode (“method”) + -isch.
Borrowed from Latin mētropolis, from Ancient Greek μητρόπολις (mētrópolis).
Borrowed from Latin metrum, derived from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron). Doublet of Meter.

From Late Middle High German mirākel, from Latin miraculum.

parole.testo: From Latin mitra, from Ancient Greek μίτρα (mítra, “headband, turban”).

From Latin modulāri + -ieren, from Latin modulus, from Latin modus

Borrowed from Latin monētae, plural of monēta, at first in grammar school slang, 18th c.

parole.significato: to criticize, to complain about something
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin monēre, from moneō (“to warn, advise”). Compare English admonish, monitor.
Latin mōnstrum, 16th c. Doublet of Monster.

From Middle High German muolter, multer, mulde, from Old High German muoltra, mulda, from Latin mulctra (“milking pail”). The modern form with -d- and without final -r- is Central and Low German; compare also Middle Low German molde, molle.

parole.significato: to multiply (transitive: perform multiplication on (a number))

parole.testo: Probably shortened from Latin animum, accusative singular of animus.
Inherited from Old High German murmul, byform with vowel assimilation of marmul, itself by liquid dissimilation from Latin marmor (“marble”). Doublet of Marmor.

From Middle High German murmeltier (14th c.), folk-etymological alteration as murmeln (“to murmur”) + Tier (“animal”) of older murmendīn, from Old High German murmunto (probably through a diminutive *murmuntīn), from Latin mūrem montis (accusative, literally “mountain rat”). Compare English marmot.

parole.significato: museum (building or institution dedicated to the protection and exhibition of items with scientific, historical, cultur…

From Latin mūsicālis. By surface analysis, Musik + -alisch.

Ca. 1700, learned borrowing from Latin mūsculus. Doublet of Muschel. One of the few mixed-declension masculines in -el (cf. Pantoffel).

parole.significato: myrobalan, any of the three myrobalans and further the whole genus Terminalia and any tree of any species in it
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin myrobalanus f, from Ancient Greek μυροβάλανος (murobálanos).
16th-century relatinization of older Mirtel, Mirten, from Middle High German mirtel, from Old High German mirtil, from Latin myrtus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos, “myrtle”).

parole.significato: meander (one of a series of regular sinuous curves, bends, loops, turns, or windings in the channel of a river, stream,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Maeander, from Ancient Greek Μαίανδρος (Maíandros) – a river in Asia Minor (present day Turkey) known for its winding course.

parole.significato: March (the third month of the Gregorian calendar, following February and preceding April, containing the northward equi…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle High German merze.

parole.significato: to copy, imitate, emulate (a person or thing)

From Middle High German narde, from Old High German narda (9th c.), from Latin nardus, from Ancient Greek νάρδος (nárdos), from a Semitic language.
Borrowed from Latin nātīvus. Cf. French nativ, English native.

From Middle High German nāwe, probably from Latin navis.

neophyte, invasive species (recently introduced plant species)

parole.significato: nickel (a silvery elemental metal with an atomic number of 28 and symbol Ni).

Partial calque of Latin membrana nictitans, influenced by nicken (“to nod”) and therefore equivalent to nicken + Haut (“skin, membrane”).

parole.significato: a representation of St. Nicholas (e.g. an actor or a figurine)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Nīcolāus. Compare English Nicholas.

parole.significato: any declinable part of speech, i.e. substantive, adjective, numeral, article, pronoun

parole.significato: 15 o'clock (the 9th hour when the first hour is set at 6 o'clock)

parole.significato: A ninth; an interval of 13 (kleine None, minor ninth) or 14 (große None, major ninth) semitones.

parole.significato: ultimate, ne plus ultra, the very best (of something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nōn plūs ultra. Doublet of Non Plus Ultra.

parole.significato: note (character indicating the length and pitch of a tone)

parole.significato: November (the eleventh month of the Gregorian calendar, following October and preceding December)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle High German november.

parole.significato: novelty (something that has not been seen before)

From Latin numerare, from numerus and -are, and from -ieren. Cognate with Hunsrik numereere.

parole.significato: sober (not drunk; serious, not playful or passionate)

From Middle High German object (14th c.), from Latin obiectum.

parole.significato: to keep someone or something under surveillance for any length of time (for a particular objective)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin observāre in the 16th century.

parole.significato: obscurant (person who seeks to prevent or hinder enquiry and the advancement of knowledge or wisdom)

From Middle High German pellez, from Old High German pelliz, from Latin pellīcia. Cognate with English pelt, Vilamovian pełc.

parole.significato: petition (formal, written request made to a parliament or an official person)
parole.testo: From Latin petītiō (“a request, petition, beseeching”).

parole.significato: to graft, engraft (insert scions from one tree, or kind of tree, etc.)
parole.testo: From Middle High German phrophen, from Old High German phrophōn, derived from phropha, from Latin propago.

parole.significato: philosophaster (a pretender to philosophy; a petty or charlatan philosopher)

From Latin physicālis. By surface analysis, Physik + -alisch.

parole.significato: trifle, bagatelle; an activity or amount that is trivial and of little consequence
parole.testo: Reduplication with ablaut of dialectal (Rhinelandic) Pill (“something small”), perhaps from Latin pilula (“pill”). See Klein-Klein for a similar construction.
Borrowed from Latin pinacothēca, from Ancient Greek πινακοθήκη (pinakothḗkē).

parole.significato: plague (affliction or hardship, particularly when seen as a divine punishment)
parole.testo: From early Middle High German plāge, from Latin plāga (“blow, wound”). The word was originally chiefly Central German, therefore sometimes secondarily adapted to the Upper German consonantism as (later) Middle High German pflāge, which form did not last, however. More at plague.
Borrowed from Latin plagiātor, from Latin plagiō + -tor, with a semantic shift; compare German Plagiat.
Inherited from Middle High German plān, from Latin plānum.

Borrowed from Latin placenta. Doublet of Palatschinke.

From French plombe + -ieren, from plomb, from Latin plumbum, from Ancient Greek μόλυβδος (mólubdos, “lead”).

parole.significato: a twisted kerchief filled with lead for domestic discipline
parole.testo: From Latin plumbum swapped with plump (“plump, clumsy”) or plumpsen (“to plump”) and Klump(e) (“lump”) + Sack (“bag”).

parole.significato: synonym of Ebene (“level surface, plain, flatland”)
parole.testo: From Middle High German plān, plāne, from Latin planum, in part through Old French plaine. Secondarily analysable as plan (“level”) + -e (noun-forming suffix). The modern umlaut is based on this reanalysis and/or influenced by Modern French plaine.
Clipping of Popo, a 17th-century reduplication of the first syllable of Podex, from Latin pōdex.
From Latin podium, from Ancient Greek πόδιον (pódion, “foot of vase”), diminutive of πούς (poús, “foot”).
From Middle High German poēte, from Latin poēta, from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs, “creator, composer”).

parole.significato: polar (pertaining to or associated with the polar regions)

From Latin polyhistor (“very learned”), from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πολυΐστωρ (poluḯstōr, “greatly learned”).

parole.significato: a member of the Pomeranian Slavic tribe
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Pomoranus, from Proto-Slavic *pomořane (“coast-dwellers”). Doublet of Pommer. See Pommern for more.

From Latin porta. Doublet of Pforte.
